item.title: copacetic
item.description:
Merriam-Webster's Word of the Day for November 22, 2026 is:

copacetic • \koh-puh-SET-ik\  • adjective

Copacetic (less commonly spelled copasetic or copesetic) describes things that are very satisfactory.

// Worry not: I assure you that everything’s copacetic.

See the entry >

Examples:

“We will be blessed with a second lunar eclipse on this night, but it won’t quite be total: at maximum, a little more than 90 percent of the moon will fall into Earth’s shadow. The event will start at 10:35 P.M. EDT, and the maximum eclipse will occur just after midnight. It won’t be as cool as the March eclipse, but the timing will be a lot more copacetic.” — Phil Plait, Scientific American, 9 Jan. 2026

Did you know?

Copacetic (with many variant spellings) is probably better known for competing theories of its origin than for any record of unconscious everyday use in American English. The first written occurrence of the word thus far detected (as copasetic) is in A Man for the Ages, a novel about the young Abraham Lincoln in rural Illinois written by Irving Bacheller and published in 1919. In the book the word is used twice by a character named Mrs. Lukins, noted for her idiosyncratic speech. Bacheller emphasizes that this word and coralapus are her peculiar property: “For a long time the word ‘coralapus’ had been a prized possession of Mrs. Lukins. … There was one other word in her lexicon which was in the nature of a jewel to be used only on special occasions. It was the word ‘copasetic.’” While coralapus passed into oblivion after the novel, it was only the beginning for copasetic—though it is far from certain that Bacheller coined the word. Until more evidence appears the origin of copacetic remains obscure.

item.title: meet-cute
item.description:
Merriam-Webster's Word of the Day for November 21, 2026 is:

meet-cute • \MEET-kyoot\  • noun

Meet-cute refers to a cute, charming, or amusing first encounter between romantic partners. A meet-cute can be such an encounter as shown in a movie or television show, or one that happens in real life.

// Their meet-cute felt as if it came straight out of a romantic comedy.

See the entry >

Examples:

“Two women, Dylan and Melanie, cross paths on an artificial beach in a near-apocalyptic meet-cute: one has emerged from the underwater pod in which she was raised, the other works at a luxury resort as a bartender… and may also be a robot.” — Natalie Zutter, Literary Hub, 2 Jan. 2026

Did you know?

Isn’t it cute how two words can be introduced to each other and become an inseparable pair soon after? Well, that’s exactly what happened when meet and cute got together in the early 1950s. The duo was spotted in The New York Times Book Review in 1952 in reference to an unexpected rendezvous: “This may well be, in magazine parlance, the neatest meet-cute of the week—the story of a ghost-writer who falls in love with a ghost.” Today the word is used often to refer to such encounters in films and television series (especially rom-coms and sitcoms). Writers of meet-cutes often develop plots by creating situations in which characters clash in personality, or by creating embarrassing situations in which two eventual romantic partners will meet, or by creating a misunderstanding between characters who will separate but become friends in the end.

item.title: ruthless
item.description:
Merriam-Webster's Word of the Day for November 20, 2026 is:

ruthless • \ROOTH-lus\  • adjective

Ruthless means "having no pity." It describes people, behaviors, circumstances, etc. regarded as cruel or merciless.

// Wolves and other large carnivores are often portrayed (and feared) as ruthless predators even as they play vital roles in their ecosystems.

See the entry >

Examples:

"One of Shakespeare's most powerful and enduring tragedies, 'Macbeth' remains an urgent and gripping story. Ambition and prophecy collide as a fateful prediction drives Macbeth into a ruthless pursuit of power, destroying everything in his path." — The Daily Gazette (Schenectady, New York), 25 Sept. 2026

Did you know?

Ruthless can be defined as "without ruth" or "having no ruth." So what, then, is ruth? The noun ruth, which is now considerably less common than ruthless, means "compassion for the misery of another," "sorrow for one's own faults," or "remorse." And, just as it is possible for one to be without ruth, it is also possible to be full of ruth. The antonym of ruthless is ruthful, meaning "full of ruth" or "tender." Ruthful can also mean "full of sorrow" or "causing sorrow." Ruth traces back to the Middle English noun ruthe, itself from ruwen, meaning "to affect with sorrow, be sorrowful, rue."

item.title: upbraid
item.description:
Merriam-Webster's Word of the Day for November 19, 2026 is:

upbraid • \up-BRAYD\  • verb

To upbraid someone is to speak to them in an angry or critical way in response to something they have done wrong—in other words, to scold them.

// The teacher upbraided the class after discovering the chalkboard erasers had been clapped all over the walls.

See the entry >

Examples:

“An industrious ant spends all summer gathering food for the cold months, while a lazy grasshopper dances and sings. Once winter hits, the grasshopper is cold and hungry, and goes begging for food from the ant, who refuses to share any of its bounty, upbraiding the grasshopper for failing to plan.” — David A. Graham, The Atlantic, 17 Apr. 2026

Did you know?

First things first: do not confuse upbraid with topknot lest you be upbraided for it. Topknot is a noun referring to a hairstyle, while upbraid is a verb (and an ancient one at that) meaning “to criticize or scold severely.” However, it may soothe your pride to know that the braid in upbraid likely comes from the same source as the verb braid, meaning “to do up (the hair) by interweaving three or more strands.” That source is the Old English word bregdan, which could be used to mean “to snatch,” “to move suddenly,” or “to plait,” i.e. “braid.” The Old English verb ūpbregdan is probably a combination of this bregdan with ūp, meaning “up.” If the connection between moving suddenly upward at someone and berating them seems obscure, you might consider upbraid to be a more formal counterpart of the expression “to get/be in someone’s face.”

item.title: hobbyhorse
item.description:
Merriam-Webster's Word of the Day for November 18, 2026 is:

hobbyhorse • \HAH-bee-horss\  • noun

Hobbyhorse refers to a topic that someone dwells on, returning to again and again, especially in conversation.

// Once he gets on his hobbyhorse and starts talking about taxes, you can't get him to discuss anything else.

See the entry >

Examples:

“This has been a hobbyhorse of mine for a while. Boston should rechristen Logan Airport to honor the unparalleled [Bill] Russell. He was Boston’s greatest sports champion, and as a brave and steadfast civil-rights leader across half a century, an even greater man.” — Mark Leibovich, The Atlantic, 14 June 2024

Did you know?

Does your favorite hobby involve a horse? Whether it does or not, the word hobby is undeniably equine: it’s a shortening of the older term hobbyhorse. And in a strange etymological twist, the word hobbyhorse is itself a product of an older word hobby that in the 1400s referred to a small or medium-sized horse, especially one that moved at a gentle pace. By the mid-1500s, hobby horse was being used to refer to a horse costume worn by a person participating in a morris dance or other performance, and then to a toy consisting of a stick with a toy horse’s head at one end that a child pretends to ride. By the next century the literal horse was unneeded, and hobbyhorse could refer to a favorite pursuit or pastime—that is, our modern hobby. From pastime, the meaning of hobbyhorse was extended to “a subject that someone returns to repeatedly, especially in conversation.” This sense is typically encountered in such phrases as “get on one’s hobbyhorse” or “ride one’s hobbyhorse.”

item.title: stolid
item.description:
Merriam-Webster's Word of the Day for November 17, 2026 is:

stolid • \STAH-lid\  • adjective

Stolid describes someone or something that has or expresses little or no emotion.

// The detective presented the facts of the case with stolid indifference.

See the entry >

Examples:

"Even the most stolid of personalities can get dragged into drama, breaking one of the biggest rules in journalism: never become the story." — Katie Rosseinsky, The Independent (United Kingdom), 15 Apr. 2026

Did you know?

Today, a person described as stolid may simply be someone who doesn't wear their feelings on their sleeve, who appears unemotional or uninterested in what is happening around them. Its use is usually descriptive, rather than disparaging. Once upon a time, however, someone calling you stolid would not be doing you a solid. Stolid comes from the Latin adjective stolidus, meaning "dull" or "stupid." It is also distantly related to the word stultify, meaning "to cause to appear or be stupid, foolish, or absurdly illogical." The earliest examples of usage for stolid, which date back to the 17th century, indicate that it too was originally associated with a lack of smarts; it was used to describe people considered foolish for their relative impassivity. By the 1800s, however, stolid was frequently appearing without such negative connotations, and it continues to be free of such overtones today.

item.title: travesty
item.description:
Merriam-Webster's Word of the Day for November 16, 2026 is:

travesty • \TRAV-uh-stee\  • noun

Travesty refers to something that is shocking, upsetting, or ridiculous because it is not what it is supposed to be, but is instead a distorted or badly inferior imitation of it. The word is often used in the phrase “a travesty of.”

// The investigation into the causes of the accident was a complete travesty.

See the entry >

Examples:

“This case is an example of the failure of our judicial system’s lack of common sense, good judgment and morality. It is nothing less than a travesty of justice.” — Richard Votapka (letter to the editor), The Stuart (Florida) News, 18 Mar. 2026

Did you know?

When disaster strikes, keeping track of which word to use seems pretty unimportant. But you don’t want to describe disastrous events as travesties, because they’re not: they’re tragedies. Travesties are terrible too, but travesty refers specifically to something that is done in a way that makes a mockery of what it’s supposed to be: for example, a contest won by the judge’s spouse could be considered a travesty. And a trial in which the defendant wasn’t allowed to present evidence could be described as a “travesty of justice.” Travesty, which can also function as a verb meaning “to make a travesty of” or “to parody,” comes from the French travestir, meaning “to disguise.” Its roots, however, wind back through Italian to the Latin vestire, meaning “to clothe” or “to dress.” Other descendants of vestire include vestment, divest, and invest.

item.title: lissome
item.description:
Merriam-Webster's Word of the Day for November 15, 2026 is:

lissome • \LISS-um\  • adjective

Lissome is an adjective used to describe someone or something characterized by easy flexibility and grace.

// He grew up wanting to emulate the lissome skaters he saw competing on television with all their acrobatic leaps and twirls.

See the entry >

Examples:

“A lissome figure in a sleek black unitard, he is a solitary presence in front of the glowing, fiery red visuals being projected on-screen.” — Mary Brennan, The Herald (Glasgow, Scotland), 30 Aug. 2026

Did you know?

Lissome (less commonly spelled lissom) is a gently altered form of its synonym, lithesome. While lissome tends to be the more popular choice these days, the two words have similar pasts. They both appeared in the 18th century, and they both trace back to the much older lithe, which first appeared in English during the 14th century and comes from an Old English word meaning “gentle.” Lissome most often describes bodies and their movements as graceful and flexible, but it is also frequently used to characterize nimble singing voices, writing styles, guitar playing, and more.

item.title: boilerplate
item.description:
Merriam-Webster's Word of the Day for November 14, 2026 is:

boilerplate • \BOY-ler-playt\  • noun

Boilerplate refers to standard or formulaic language, a meaning that comes from an earlier meaning still in use: syndicated material supplied to newspapers in matrix or plate form.

// The last paragraph of the contract was legal boilerplate.

See the entry >

Examples:

"New Orleans is where the food, music, history and culture are unlike anywhere else in the world. That's not travel-guide boilerplate—it's what hits you the moment you step into the French Quarter and feel the city operating on its own rhythm." — Lauren Schuster, The Miami Herald, 8 Apr. 2026

Did you know?

In the days before computers, small newspapers around the U.S. relied heavily on feature stories, editorials, and other printed material supplied by large publishing syndicates. The syndicates delivered that copy on metal plates with the type already in place so the local papers wouldn't have to set it. Printers apparently dubbed those syndicated plates "boiler plates" because of their resemblance to the plating used in making steam boilers. Soon boilerplate came to refer to the printed material on the plates as well as to the plates themselves. Because boilerplate stories were often more filler—material used to fill extra space in a column or page of a newspaper to increase its size—than important or informative news, the word acquired negative connotations and gained the "standardized or formulaic language" sense widely used today.

item.title: impertinent
item.description:
Merriam-Webster's Word of the Day for November 13, 2026 is:

impertinent • \im-PER-tuh-nunt\  • adjective

Impertinent is a formal word describing someone or something that is rude and showing a lack of respect.

// The band stopped doing interviews after years of journalists asking invasive and impertinent questions.

See the entry >

Examples:

“On Friday night, I discovered that the plans I had for Saturday morning were not going to work out, so I decided to go fishing instead. It was too late to hitch up with a fishing buddy, and it would be impertinent to ask permission to fish on someone’s private property at such a late hour, so I decided to go by myself to the public section of the Soque River.” — Bill Hager, The White County (Georgia) News, 7 July 2026

Did you know?

A pertinent statement or remark is one that pertains—that is, is relevant—to the subject at hand. It stands to reason, therefore, that impertinent could be used to describe things that are irrelevant. Indeed, “not pertinent” is the word’s oldest meaning, dating to the 15th century. A pertinent question: how did a word meaning “irrelevant” come to also describe someone as rude (now the more common sense of impertinent)? The answer comes down to the particular quality of rudeness on display. Burping loudly while your teacher is giving a lecture, for example, would be rude, but unlikely to be called impertinent. Raising your hand mid-lecture to ask where your teacher purchased such a ridiculous sweater, however, would be impertinent, i.e. such a question is rude because it in no way pertains to the matter at hand in a classroom.
